title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: 28 officials targeted in recalls over data center votes—what it means for your bills and land.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy—the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're diving into growing recall pressure on local officials and how these fights are reshaping communities from the U.P. to southwest Michigan.
That's the big one today.
A new Bridge Michigan analysis shows at least 28 officials in eight communities have faced recall efforts tied directly to their data center votes.
Only one of those recalls has even made it onto the November ballot so far.
Exactly. These aren't abstract policy fights anymore—they're hitting ballots and forcing neighbors to choose sides on power plants disguised as server farms.
Why now? What's changed that has residents organizing recalls instead of just showing up at meetings?

The scale. Proposals are multiplying fast in western Michigan townships and places like Marquette County, and people are realizing what one big facility can do to their electric rates and water supply.
Walk me through the stakes on power and water. How much are we talking?
A single large data center can pull as much electricity as a small city and use millions of gallons of water for cooling. Locals worry their bills go up to subsidize that demand.
And farmland gets paved over or rezoned in the process.
Right. Rural townships that voted to keep things quiet and agricultural are suddenly staring at traffic, noise, and lost open space.
So the recalls are a direct reaction to those votes approving or blocking projects.
Yes. Bridge Michigan tracked efforts in eight communities. Most haven't qualified for the ballot yet, but the pressure is real and it's statewide.
What happens next if more recalls qualify?
Special elections could flip boards and change the rules mid-game. Developers are already suing places like Gibraltar over moratoriums, so the legal fights will keep going.
Is this the first wave or have we seen recalls over data centers before in Michigan?

This analysis is the clearest statewide picture so far. Earlier fights were more localized—noise complaints in one township, tax breaks in another—but now it's coordinated enough to hit multiple officials at once.
And only one made the ballot. That tells me organizers are still learning how to gather signatures fast enough.
Or that many of these votes happened recently and the clock is still running on the petition process.
For listeners 30 or 50 miles away, why should they care about what happens in these specific eight communities?
Because the precedent travels. If one township blocks a project on water concerns, the next developer just moves down the road to the next willing board.
And the power demand doesn't disappear—it just shifts the burden to the regional grid.
Exactly. Higher rates and more strain on infrastructure hit everyone who shares the same utility territory.
So the recall pressure is really about who gets to decide the future of these towns before the next big proposal lands.
That's the heart of it. And with more projects in the pipeline, expect the signature drives to keep coming.
We'll watch which of those eight communities actually get recalls on the ballot and what the campaigns look like.
Now let's hit the other stories making news this weekend.
Starting with today—Kluver Road township officials rejected a server farm permit after residents raised noise, traffic, and water worries.
That keeps the rural area free of large-scale facilities for now.
Same day in South Haven, neighbors are fighting a rezoning that could open the door to a data center on the Baseline property.
They're citing the same concerns—noise, traffic, and strain on local services—and the outcome here could influence nearby townships facing similar proposals.
Yesterday in Forsyth Township, hundreds packed the hall to grill officials on power rates, water use, and even rumored military ties to the projects in Marquette County.
First real public look at the scale for Upper Peninsula residents.
Also yesterday, a developer sued Gibraltar to overturn that year-long data center moratorium.
Wayne County residents could see delayed tax revenue and jobs if the suit succeeds. It tests how far local governments can slow these facilities.
In Mason, the firm behind the proposed data center finally got named.
Ingham County residents now have a clearer target for questions about water, noise, and grid impact.
St. Joseph County is weighing its own two-year freeze on new projects while leaders study roads, water, and electricity.
Residents there worry about higher utility bills and lost farmland—another potential model for southwest Michigan townships.
In Saline, dozens showed up at a coffee hour to question leaders about electric bills, water use, and lost tax revenue if projects win breaks.
The issue is clearly becoming a flashpoint in Washtenaw County.
Hyperscale Data sold $43 million in Bitcoin—685 BTC—to cut debt and fund its Michigan buildout.
Crypto volatility now directly feeding local power and water demands.
And on Friday, Palmyra Township residents in Lenawee County pushed back on plans over fears of spiking electric bills and constant noise.
Anyone within 50 miles could feel higher utility costs if those projects move without stricter limits.
That's a lot of activity in just two days.
It shows how quickly the issue is spreading beyond the initial hotspots.
On deck for listeners who want to get involved—no major public meetings are listed for the weekend itself.
But township boards across the state will be back in session next week. Check your local clerk for agendas on rezoning and moratorium votes.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Recall Push Grows as Data Center Battles Spread Across Michigan Townships
